messages.author: 3b0346de291d44f7
messages.subject: Spatial binomial model overfitting
parts:
Dear INLA group,

I am trying to fit a simple binomial model with bym2 prior specification to estimate prevalence. My issue is the resultant fitted values from the model are identical to the crude prevalence values. I had hoped some Bayesian spatial shrinkage/smoothing would happen but this does not seem to be the case. I am not sure if it is because of the code I am using or if the data will not allow for it. I tried various priors and this is still an issue. I think the model is overfitting the data. 

I have run examples from different textbooks and this issue does not appear. I have attached a simple reprex for you to see. Your assistance is appreciated.

Kind regards,
John

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial binomial model overfitting
parts:
yes, you get a 'perfect fit'. the graph looks ok.

I think this due to, too many parameters. you have 41 regions/data-points.

to this you have intercept + 2 regression coefficients, plus 2 x 41 parameters
in the 'bym2' model.

maybe, you'll be find using 'besag' for the 'bym2' ?

hmm, even changing it into

+ f(ID, model = "besag", hyper = list(prec = list(prior =
"pc.prec", param = c(0.05, 0.01))), graph = g),

did not help.


* you have to use integer values for 'population', really...

* the covariates is better to scale somehow, so they are more centered and not
to extreme. this is the easy way out, but you may do something more sensible

mod.bym2 <- inla(num_cases ~ scale(w_mean_age) + scale(mean_income_k)

messages.author: 3b0346de291d44f7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial binomial model overfitting
parts:
Thank you for taking time to look at my problem. I had previously tried just running the model on the covariates only but felt that it could be improved by adding spatial random effects.

If I may ask, wouldn't the issue of overfitting persist regardless of the number of observations/regions for this type of modelling (BYM2)? For example, if I had 1000 observations, that would imply at least 2000 parameters in the model. I followed the same analysis steps the authors from this paper took and found they had similar overfitting issues (however only to 3 decimal places rather than my 5), although they had more than 6000 observations.

Is the BYM specification not ideal in general for this type of data?

Kind regards,
John
